doc.title: Daryl Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2024

title: Getting the Waldorf job in 1994 and how to keep a steady gig
summary: On the day of her first Marian McPartland show she was called to play the Waldorf lobby, a paid audition that became fourteen years; she gives advice on keeping gigs and recalls the Sheridan Center.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: How do you keep a steady gig? I think that’s just basically my question. Or maybe I can turn it around.

By, you know first of all by getting a steady gig like here’s a case in point: The Waldorf. And I remember the day so well. I have to get this in. ’94 I was doing my first show with © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

Marian McPartland recording at the studio down in the West 30s, and but I was younger then so I wasn’t as crazy and nervous as I am now, so I did that but also just before I left I got a call from an agent who booked The Waldorf asking me if I could go in and play, apparently the piano was in the middle of the lobby at that point. And I said, “Okay, sure, fine.” So after I did her show, and it was the first one where — her format you know of course. There’s two pianos, she talks, we gab a little bit and then she makes it sound like we’re doing it like just off the cuff but of course — “So what should we do for the second song?” You know it’s very organized. Well, not the actual playing but at least the order. So after all that I go to The Waldorf and I play in the lobby the Cole Porter piano. I’m not even sure if I sang because I don’t even remember if they had a microphone. Maybe they did. Come to find out that a very good singer/pianist I knew, a colleague, whatever she did it’s one of those things where the general manager had walked by, noticed her, and then gave the directive, “She’s got to go.” Now she was, she was a bit kooky, she wore hats and she had long nails and a little eccentric. Whatever it was I feel bad for her although she moved south and she did very well after that. But I got hired. It was like a paid audition, and then I was there for fourteen years. So to answer your actual question, a combination of things. Maybe prepare and bring some things in that you want to play and maybe something you’re going to read, you know, depending on if no one’s paying attention that’s a good time to do that. And you try to have some prep on who this crowd is. They’re probably — at like The Sheridan Center I was right across the street from the show “Cats.” That was, you know, the theater district. And I actually, I actually told the actress who sang it every night, I said, “I sing this song eight times in a five hour gig, every night.” [sings] “Midnight —” so yeah, you’ve got to be prepared for that. It depends on the place. In The Waldorf I was up in the Cocktail Terrace, that’s what they called it, and it was the main entrance of the beautiful art deco lobby. Who knows what it’s going to be like. It has been many years now just in construction. The rumor is it’s planning to open again soon. But during that time I was — actually right playing and below was the main entrance, One Park Avenue. People would come in and go through that way, and then the Lexington Avenue entrance people might come through. Some would stay but it was a really good place to go across, particularly if you’re going to Grand Central Station. You go through the Waldorf and then you get to the stop. So I had a relationship just with people coming either from Lexington to Park, looking up and waving, or Park to Lexington. I had a relationship with the staff. Everything from the bartenders, some of the managers, and more interesting, the people who were there in security or someone who — she had the most gorgeous face — who was polishing the railing of the staircases. Brass railing and stuff, you know, every day. I mean it was such a whole other world. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
